items.title: METR publishes independent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic (October 2026)
items.summary_en: According to search-result excerpts of METR's report, METR estimates that benchmark progress for Anthropic's models has run at about 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate (95% CI roughly 1.5-2.8x). METR attributes roughly 80% of the current acceleration to AI, and says it found no convincing bottlenecks to continued rapid progress. METR staff reportedly spent eleven weeks on the work.
items.notes: Inside the preferred window. Direct fetch of metr.org failed (domain not resolvable in this session), so details come from a search-engine excerpt of the METR page, not the full text. Figures need checking against the original before publication. Per that excerpt, METR's own caveats are: the 80% attribution is a subjective judgment with substantial uncertainty; some evidence (key intermediate measures, algorithmic-progress estimates) was shared with METR but not described publicly; parts of the report are redacted. Likely a companion to the item metr-2026-11-05-rd-section-anthropic-risk-report-review.

items.title: METR reviews the 'Risks from automated R&D' section of Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report
items.summary_en: According to a search-result excerpt, METR agrees that internally deployed models posed low risk of directly automating R&D in key domains as of July 15. METR argues, however, that Anthropic's claim that models had not crossed early-warning thresholds rests on contestable judgment calls. It also says the public report likely understates the acceleration that was occurring.
items.notes: Inside the preferred window. Based on a search excerpt only (direct fetch blocked). This is a divergence between an evaluator and a developer (Anthropic) on how to interpret thresholds; present both views side by side and cite Anthropic's own Risk Report via the Anthropic collector. METR's own methodology caveats could not be read in full.

items.title: METR summary of predeployment evaluation of GPT-5.6 Sol (background only)
items.summary_en: According to a search excerpt, METR's evaluation on its Time Horizon 1.1 suite gave a point estimate of about 71 hours with a very wide 95% interval (roughly 13 to 11,400 hours). METR reportedly says the result depends heavily on how model cheating attempts are detected and treated, and does not treat the numbers as a robust measurement.
items.notes: Predates the 2026-08-29 run, so it is NOT new this period. Listed only as context for the time-horizon measurement caveats (saturating task suite, sensitivity to analysis choices, as METR itself noted in a March 2026 note). It may already have been covered by an earlier run; the synthesis step should avoid double-counting. Based on a search excerpt only.
